newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. Fed seen raising rates by 25 bp - SocGen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed seen raising rates by 25 bp - SocGen.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve will likely raise interest rates by 25 basis points when its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Wednesday, SocGen-Crosby Securities (HK) Ltd said on Tuesday.
"We see a series of two 25-basis-point increases during 1997, which will put short-term interest rates at about five to 5.75 percent," SocGen economist Clive McDonnell told reporters.
The rate increases would come in the first half of the year because of worries over the U.S. inflation outlook, he said.
"We are quite concerned about the outlook for inflation in the U.S., specifically focusing on the labour market," he said. "The recent increase in wages was a cause of concern."
McDonnell said the period of spare capacity in the U.S. labour market had now lapsed.
"That is going to result in upward pressure in unit labour costs and I feel that has already come through in headline wage costs," he said.
Prompt action by the Fed would boost confidence, particularly in the bond market, McDonnell said.
"If they get there early enough, that should quash the inflation pressures that are building and allow the long end of the yield curve to rally towards the end of the year," he said.
McDonnell forecast the 30-year U.S. Treasuries would rally, bringing the yield to six to 6.2 percent the end of the year.
Bond prices rose on Monday on hopes the Fed would hold rates steady. The 30-year Treasury rose 19/32 of a point, lowering the yield to 6.74 percent from 6.79 percent.

McDonnell said his view contrasted with International Monetary Fund forecasts of steady U.S. rates during 1997, but he stressed the potential increases would not represent a drastic change in the U.S. central bank's monetary policy.
"It will be a fine-tuning of interest rates rather than a tightening of monetary policy," he said.
